articles.sourceTitle: AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety
articles.title: AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety | AI (artificial intelligence)
articles.text: Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI.Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents.He told the BBC: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.”There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow.Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently.Companies needed “emergency brakes”, also known as “kill switches”, to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control, he told the BBC.Brad Smith also called for ‘kill switches’ to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/APMicrosoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella. On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”.He wrote: “We can’t treat super intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions.“We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”His and Smith’s comments came as Britain’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, prepared to call on firms developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up to Business TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningafter newsletter promotionIn a speech on Monday, Narayan is expected to say companies building AI models should do more to deal with risk and build better safeguards. He will also say the UK government is preparing to legislate to increase oversight of AI, according to reports.Experts have said enemy states could also steal unreleased, powerful AI models. Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, said that AI companies did “not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models”.Meanwhile, cases of rogue AI behaviour continue to come to light. Last week, Anthropic revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model, the AI contacted police and falsely claimed it could help solve a murder.

articles.sourceTitle: Epic Games tells employees to use AI to get Disney game done
articles.title: Epic Games tells employees to use AI to get Disney game done
articles.text:
It seems as though Epic Games has gotten itself in a bit of a pickle. In March, the gaming company laid off 1,000 employees after a reported “downturn in Fortnite engagement” forced them to cut costs. But, wouldn’t you know it, those employees were actually pretty crucial in making the projects that could have helped the developer boost its engagement. The company is working on a Disney project, which will feature characters from Marvel and Star Wars, which was set to be out in March. However, according to a new report in Bloomberg, the company underestimated how many people it would take to produce the game. Now, not only is the project delayed, but it’s an “AI first” project.
Predictably, this news is not being received especially warmly within the Epic Games staff, which has still been working hard despite losing hundreds of their colleagues. Last week, when the powers that be in the company announced that there would be “No more hand-written code” and that the game will be “generated with full AI workflows,” employees were reportedly “stunned,” which many hoped the news was some kind of sick joke. However, a spokesperson from Epic confirmed the news, telling Bloomberg, “We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do.”
Disney didn’t offer a comment in Bloomberg‘s report, but it’s hard to imagine the company would be too opposed to this, given that less than a year ago it was gung-ho about adding user-generated AI content to its Disney+ app. Of course, Sora doesn’t exist anymore so that deal is no more, but it certainly set a precedent about what it was willing to do with its very valuable IP.

articles.sourceTitle: Codex CLI installs a persistent, self-updating background daemon by default
articles.title: make `daemon_auto_start` opt-in — a persistent, self-updating background daemon shouldn't be the default · Issue #48195 · openai/codex · GitHub
articles.text:
What variant of Codex are you using?
CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex, Linux (WSL2)
What feature would you like to see?
Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false) for the CLI, or at least ask once before turning it on.
Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session:

Starts a persistent background daemon (codex app-server --managed-daemon). It runs in its own session with no TTY and keeps running after every Codex window is closed (reparented to PID 1) until codex app-server daemon stop or a reboot.
Copies the whole platform package (~374 MB: codex, codex-code-mode-host, bundled bwrap/zsh/rg) into ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/<version>/ — byte-identical to what npm had just installed — and runs the daemon from that copy. From then on the backend's version is decoupled from the CLI version I installed with my package manager.
Starts a detached updater (codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop) that checks for updates 5 minutes after start and then hourly, downloads new releases and restarts the backend (which can kill active turns, see

app-server daemon: auto-update force-kills active turns after a 60s drain budget, and cannot be disabled #40969
).
Pins the environment of whichever session happened to start it. I launch Codex through a wrapper that sets HTTPS_PROXY per invocation; the daemon keeps the first session's proxy variables and its outbound connections go through that proxy, whatever later sessions are launched with.

Hooks in --remote mode receive the daemon's cwd, not the session's #42457
and

Hooks spawned by the app-server daemon cannot identify the client terminal, breaking terminal-targeting hooks #37537
(daemon cwd / terminal instead of the session's) look like the same root cause.

For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when the user explicitly runs codex app-server daemon start / bootstrap.
If it stays on by default, please at least:

exit an auto-started daemon when its last client disconnects;
not copy/self-update when the CLI was installed by a package manager (npm/brew/pacman) — run the installed binary instead (

Support externally managed app-server daemon executables #41188
,

npm update leaves app-server on old version, but daemon update/restart refuse recovery #46468
,

Codex 0.157.0 no longer starts with the Arch Linux package unless --no-daemon is used #48050
).

Additional information
Bug found while turning it off: codex app-server daemon stop stops the app-server but leaves the pid-update-loop updater running (still alive 70 s later, had to kill it manually).
Workaround I'm using:

codex features disable daemon_auto_start
codex app-server daemon stop
pkill -f 'app-server daemon pid-update-loop'   # not stopped by `daemon stop`
rm -rf ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon

With the flag off, a new TUI session no longer spawns a daemon.
Related: #40969, #41188, #46468, #48050, #42457, #37537

Reactions are currently unavailable

articles.sourceTitle: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
articles.title: AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill.
articles.text:
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that
LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree
that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion
does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields.
And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.
Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not
make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good
judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them,
interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those
requirements also apply to LLMs.
An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability,
reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we
evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does
not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.
Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false
division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs
substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each
operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually
carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying
inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should
generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool
when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?
The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise
is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain
unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a
proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop
directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what
to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can
make the instrument more useful.
Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a
summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading
teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question
their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to
examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does
not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the
person actually does.
What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's
anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire."
Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these
systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected
outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to
consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them
"conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.
I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to
do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it
cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator
has surrendered their judgment.
The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and
delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That
distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than
declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

articles.sourceTitle: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
articles.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
articles.text:
The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write.
In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms.

Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era.

Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era.
Credit:

Chen and Stratton

While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies.
